summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework for passports, entry screening and federal identity documents; the findings below are specific to the state.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment dated July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking, lists North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates, which forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents.

Birth-certificate gender markers are effectively closed. A 2023 North Dakota law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states. Accompanying regulations to the May 2023 bill were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to people who have undergone a sex conversion operation.

State identity documents follow a different rule from birth certificates. The North Dakota Department of Transportation updates the gender marker on a driver's licence or state ID upon receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition.

North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Employment protection rests solely on Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020), which holds that federal Title VII covers gender identity, and on limited city-level protection: Grand Forks has protected city employees and applicants and rental housing since 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students despite institutional non-discrimination policies.

State hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Prosecution of bias-motivated violence on that basis depends on the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a North Dakota bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023.

School and collegiate sport is closed to transgender girls. 2021 legislation banning participation in girls' school sports teams passed 69 to 25 in the House and 27 to 20 in the Senate and was vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021; in April 2023 two bills were signed into law banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively.

An April 2023 law, signed by the Governor and effective 1 July 2023, explicitly allows restriction of transgender people's use of public bathrooms in many state-run facilities.

A May 2023 statute, HB 1522, relating to preferred pronouns and accommodations for transgender students, was signed by the Governor with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023 and effective 1 July 2023. It forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use, and requires disclosure of transgender students to parents in state-run schools. It followed a March 2023 bill that would have required parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms, which was vetoed.

A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counsellors in North Dakota.

Marriages that North Dakota classes as same-sex are recognised under the national rule established by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015. Within the state, the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalised same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020. State law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate on the basis of sincerely held religious belief, which affects a trans resident or visitor seeking to adopt through such an agency.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2020 platform adopted by the state's Republican delegates opposed any civil-rights protections for LGBTQ people and accused transgender people "of preying on women" and LGBTQ people of "recruiting children". Many Republican delegates condemned the platform, and Governor Doug Burgum called it "divisive and divisional", stating that all North Dakotans deserve to be treated equally and free of discrimination.

A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found that 78 percent of North Dakota residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 22 percent opposed.

Several tribal nations in North Dakota record third-gender or gender-non-conforming roles with distinct terms in their own languages, including the skuxát of the Arikara, the miati and mihdeke of the Hidatsa and Mandan, and the wįktą, winkta and wíŋkte of the Assiniboine, Dakota and Lakota. The source states that perceptions of gender and sexuality within Native American tribes differ from those of people of European descent, both historically and at present.

Custody law in North Dakota carries a documented history on this point: a 1980s state Supreme Court ruling made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody cases because of societal prejudices, a position reversed in 2003.
localsOnly:
Protections for North Dakota residents are patchy and mostly local. Grand Forks has protected city employees and applicants and rental housing on gender identity and sexual orientation since 2013; Fargo has protected city employees on sexual orientation since 2001 and Jamestown does likewise. A Senate bill of 17 February 2015 banning sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed 25 to 22 but failed in the House.

State statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation either, and the state hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, leaving federal prosecution under the 2009 statute as the only bias-crime route.

Adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, but state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to refuse on sincerely held religious belief.

A March 2023 bill that passed to allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objection alone awaited gubernatorial action at the point the source was written.

The June 2021 committee regulation banning conversion therapy applies to social workers, psychologists and counsellors licensed in the state, and is the principal state-level protective instrument in this record.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the regulations contemplated by the 2023 birth-certificate statute were ever adopted is unresolved in the sources. The record shows that accompanying regulations were rejected and that a 2008 regulation requiring a sex conversion operation remains in force, but no later regulatory action is sourced, so the operative standard cannot be stated with certainty beyond that point.

Enforcement of the April 2023 bathroom-restriction law is not sourced. No arrest, citation or complaint under it in North Dakota appears in the inventory, and the record contains no dated incident of violence against a trans person in the state.

The July 2026 assessment ranks North Dakota by legislative risk, not by incident count, and supplies no per-capita or population denominator; its placement among the "worst states" is a measure of bills enacted, not of measured violence.

The final disposition of the March 2023 religious-refusal bill is unresolved in the sources, which record it as awaiting gubernatorial action.

Whether the penalty provision attached to HB 1522 has been used against any student, teacher or school employee is not sourced.
